## 1) Chart type
A **faceted pictogram / icon array chart** (small-multiple waffle-style display), using person-shaped state icons.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples** by voter profile:
  - The No-ID Voter
  - The Working-Parent Voter
  - The Procrastinating Voter
  - The Eager Student Voter
  - The Convicted-Felon Voter
- Within each facet, the display is split into **two grouped panels**:
  - **Could Not Vote**
  - **Could Vote**
- No stacking in the usual bar/area sense; icons are arranged in compact grids/groups.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Voter profile / voter type (e.g., No-ID, Working-Parent, Procrastinating, Eager Student, Convicted-Felon) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting; panel title |
| Voting ability status (“Could Not Vote” vs “Could Vote”) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped sub-panel position within each facet; text label |
| Number of states | Quantitative | Large numeric label above each group; also implied by count of icons |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual icon/mark; state abbreviation label on each icon |
| State House majority party (Republican vs Democratic) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of icon (red vs blue) |

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted pictogram / icon array chart** (small-multiple waffle-style display), using person-shaped state icons.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples** by voter profile:
  - The No-ID Voter
  - The Working-Parent Voter
  - The Procrastinating Voter
  - The Eager Student Voter
  - The Convicted-Felon Voter
- Within each facet, the display is split into **two grouped panels**:
  - **Could Not Vote**
  - **Could Vote**
- No stacking in the usual bar/area sense; icons are arranged in compact grids/groups.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Voter profile / voter type (e.g., No-ID, Working-Parent, Procrastinating, Eager Student, Convicted-Felon) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting; panel title |
| Voting ability status (“Could Not Vote” vs “Could Vote”) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped sub-panel position within each facet; text label |
| Number of states | Quantitative | Large numeric label above each group; also implied by count of icons |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual icon/mark; state abbreviation label on each icon |
| State House majority party (Republican vs Democratic) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of icon (red vs blue) |

A **faceted pictogram / icon array chart** (small-multiple waffle-style display), using person-shaped state icons.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples** by voter profile:
  - The No-ID Voter
  - The Working-Parent Voter
  - The Procrastinating Voter
  - The Eager Student Voter
  - The Convicted-Felon Voter
- Within each facet, the display is split into **two grouped panels**:
  - **Could Not Vote**
  - **Could Vote**
- No stacking in the usual bar/area sense; icons are arranged in compact grids/groups.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Voter profile / voter type (e.g., No-ID, Working-Parent, Procrastinating, Eager Student, Convicted-Felon) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting; panel title |
| Voting ability status (“Could Not Vote” vs “Could Vote”) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped sub-panel position within each facet; text label |
| Number of states | Quantitative | Large numeric label above each group; also implied by count of icons |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual icon/mark; state abbreviation label on each icon |
| State House majority party (Republican vs Democratic) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of icon (red vs blue) |

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted pictogram / icon array chart** (small-multiple waffle-style display), using person-shaped state icons.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples** by voter profile:
  - The No-ID Voter
  - The Working-Parent Voter
  - The Procrastinating Voter
  - The Eager Student Voter
  - The Convicted-Felon Voter
- Within each facet, the display is split into **two grouped panels**:
  - **Could Not Vote**
  - **Could Vote**
- No stacking in the usual bar/area sense; icons are arranged in compact grids/groups.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Voter profile / voter type (e.g., No-ID, Working-Parent, Procrastinating, Eager Student, Convicted-Felon) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting; panel title |
| Voting ability status (“Could Not Vote” vs “Could Vote”) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped sub-panel position within each facet; text label |
| Number of states | Quantitative | Large numeric label above each group; also implied by count of icons |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual icon/mark; state abbreviation label on each icon |
| State House majority party (Republican vs Democratic) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of icon (red vs blue) |

raw_comment:
In this graph, I noticed the following:
In regards to procrastinating voters, only 33% could vote. In comparison to convicted-felon voters, there is only an 8% increase in states that could vote. Moreover, between no ID and Working parent voters, only 54% and 47% could vote, respectively. While there is a majority of Democrats able to vote in the group of convicted-felon voters, the eager students that are able to vote have a Republican majority. 

I wonder why the Republican population has a greater amount of states not voting, especially considering that they are the majority party in the United States. Also, why do two groups have a summation of 51 while the others have a summation of 50? Do some groups consider TheDistrict of Columbia? 

I think this graph has a lot to do with the rise of hyperpartisanship, and how a majority of Americans feel reluctant to vote (as a result). I would title this graph: "Who is participating in our pluralist republic?" or "Apolitical strata limits the representation of the whole".

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you Wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  Plus, share with us a catchy headline.
On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these infographics and much more.

Learn different perspectives when you read what other students have to say about your response.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted pictogram / icon array chart** (small-multiple waffle-style display), using person-shaped state icons.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples** by voter profile:
  - The No-ID Voter
  - The Working-Parent Voter
  - The Procrastinating Voter
  - The Eager Student Voter
  - The Convicted-Felon Voter
- Within each facet, the display is split into **two grouped panels**:
  - **Could Not Vote**
  - **Could Vote**
- No stacking in the usual bar/area sense; icons are arranged in compact grids/groups.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Voter profile / voter type (e.g., No-ID, Working-Parent, Procrastinating, Eager Student, Convicted-Felon) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting; panel title |
| Voting ability status (“Could Not Vote” vs “Could Vote”) | Categorical/nominal | Grouped sub-panel position within each facet; text label |
| Number of states | Quantitative | Large numeric label above each group; also implied by count of icons |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual icon/mark; state abbreviation label on each icon |
| State House majority party (Republican vs Democratic) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of icon (red vs blue) |

- No stacking in the usual bar/area sense; icons are arranged in compact grids/groups.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

raw_comment:

Meanwhile, all the states that could not vote for each section were Republican. Also majority of the eager student voters who could vote were from Republican states. It seems that the more educated states (working parent and eager student voters) were Republican states.
I wonder why for each section, the two numbers add up to 51 states instead of 50. Because there are 50 states in the U.S., so I don't understand why there are 51 states accounted for in this graph. Was D.C. counted as a state?
A catchy headline for this graph could be "Republican states vote less"
